Today students meet the narrator of that adaptation and look for the first signs of a modern myth in Percy's own voice.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories pass on shared values and fears. A narrator's voice and word choices shape how readers see a character and what ideas they expect the story to explore.","futureLessons":"Lesson 5 (Core Writing) uses Chapter 1 evidence to practice explanatory paragraphs with topic sentences, relevant evidence and a concluding statement. Today's inferences about what Percy values and fears are the first evidence for a theme they will track across the novel."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"envy","definition":"to wish you had what someone else has or could do what someone else can do","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"recognize","definition":"to know someone or something because you have seen it before; to understand what something is","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"frayed","definition":"worn, with loose threads or edges showing","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"expelled","definition":"officially forced to leave a school","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"probation","definition":"a trial period in which a person must behave well or face a serious consequence","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"threatened","definition":"warned that something bad will happen","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"spawn","definition":"the offspring of a creature; in a joking or insulting way, a child of something bad","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"detention","definition":"a punishment in which a student must stay after school or during free time","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"immortal","definition":"living forever; never dying","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"dyslexia","definition":"a learning difference that makes reading and spelling harder","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mortal","definition":"a being who will eventually die","tier":"support"},{"word":"mythology","definition":"a collection of myths, or the study of myths","tier":"support"},{"word":"transform","definition":"to change into something different","tier":"support"},{"word":"sarcastic","definition":"saying the opposite of what you mean, often to mock or joke","tier":"support"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the attitude a writer or narrator shows toward a subject","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 1–8"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they know about \"normal\" and about Riordan's goals for myths, and get curious about a narrator who warns readers away from his own story.","activities":[{"id":"launch-normal-turn-and-talk","title":"What Does \"Normal\" Mean?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner: What does it mean to be a \"normal\" kid? Is being normal something people want, fear, or both? Be ready to share one idea."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does it mean to be a \"normal\" kid, and why might someone want to be one?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Normal means fitting in, like having friends and not getting in trouble. Someone might want it because standing out can feel lonely or scary."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Last time, we heard Rick Riordan explain that myths carry what people value and fear. Today we meet Percy, the narrator of a modern myth. Listen for what he wants readers to believe about normal kids, and about himself."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 90 seconds of talk and 2 shares. You want students curious, not finished. Page numbers can vary slightly by edition; use the opening of Chapter 1 as your anchor if yours differs."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students use morphology to build myth-related word meanings, then preview the unit vocabulary they will confirm in context while reading.","activities":[{"id":"lab-morphology-word-building","title":"Word Building: mort-, -ology, trans-","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.4.d","L.6.5"],"routine":"Word-Building Routine","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Watch the word parts on the board: mort- (death), -ology (study of), trans- (across, change). Work with a partner to build and explain each word, then check your meaning against a dictionary or the glossary."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Think aloud: \"Word parts are clues, but I always verify. I build a meaning from the parts, then check it against a sentence or a dictionary.\" Write *mort-* and *immortal* on the board. Circle *im-* (not), *mort* (death), and *-al* (having to do with)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If *mort* means death, what does *immortal* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"*Im-* means not, so immortal means not dying, someone who lives forever, like the Greek gods."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What would *mortal* mean, and why might a myth need both words?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortal means someone who will die, like humans. Myths need both because they are about gods who live forever and people who don't."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"The word part *-ology* means \"the study of.\" What does *mythology* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mythology means the study of myths, or a group of myths, like Greek mythology."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Trans-* means across or change. What do *transform* and *transport* have in common?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both are about moving or changing. Transport moves something across a place, and transform changes it into something else. Percy might be changing in this story."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep this to 5 minutes. Students use word parts to predict, then verify. If a prediction is off, praise the thinking and fix it with the dictionary. Connect to Spanish cognates: *mortal*, *inmortal*, *mitología*, *transformar*, *transportar*."}]},{"id":"lab-vocab-organizer","title":"Unit Vocabulary Organizer: Preview and Confirm in Context","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d","L.6.6"],"routine":"Vocabulary Graphic Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Add all ten words: envy, recognize, frayed, expelled, probation, threatened, spawn, detention, immortal, dyslexia. For *immortal*, record the word parts and meaning from the word-building routine. For the other nine, write only the word and page number for now. You will confirm each meaning in context as you meet it in the text."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Ten words is a lot, so we will go deep on some and light on the rest. *Immortal* and *envy* we will study closely today. For *recognize, frayed, expelled, probation, threatened, spawn, detention* and *dyslexia*, we will pause to confirm the meaning as the words appear in the read-aloud."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *expelled*, *probation* and *detention*. What do they have in common, and what does that make you predict about Percy?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They are all school punishments. That makes me predict Percy gets in trouble a lot at school."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Do not define the words now. The goal is to preview and notice patterns. Later in the lesson, students will check meanings against context (L.6.4.a) and confirm with a dictionary or glossary (L.6.4.d)."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners connect word parts and word families to meaning, and use reference tools to verify.","sayAsk":"Say: \"Mortal and immortal are opposites. Say each word with me.\" Ask: \"What does the part *im-* tell you?\" Frames: \"The word part ___ means ___.\" \"I think ___ means ___ because ___.\" \"The dictionary confirms ___.\"","watchFor":"If students guess a meaning without word parts, then point to one part and ask what it means. Success: students name the word part, state a predicted meaning, and check it against a reference."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: using word parts to predict meaning","tryTry":"","tryThis":"Give a partially filled word-part chart and have students say the meaning of each part aloud before combining. Offer the frame: \"___ means ___, so the whole word means ___.\""},{"situation":"Ready for extension: morphology","tryThis":"Have students find other words with *mort-*, *-ology* or *trans-* (mortality, biology, translate) and explain how the parts shape the meaning."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students listen to a modeled read-aloud of pp. 1–8 and track what Percy says and how. Part B: Students analyze how Percy's informal, sarcastic word choices create tone and a first impression. Part C: Students make evidence-based inferences and predictions about Percy as a hero or \"problem\" figure and name an emerging theme.","activities":[{"id":"lia-read-aloud-think-aloud","title":"Part A: Teacher Read Aloud and Think-Alouds (pp. 1–8)","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3","RL.6.6","RL.6.10","L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d"],"routine":"Read Aloud with Think-Aloud and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Follow along in your book as your teacher reads aloud. Annotate: underline what Percy says about himself and about \"normal\" kids, put a star by any word that shows his attitude, and circle each vocabulary word when you hear it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Model engaging fluency: slow down at the opening warning, add a dry, sarcastic edge to Percy's lines, and pause at the stopping points below. Stop only 3–4 times so the story keeps moving."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 1, after the opening warning (\"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood...\"): \"Notice he starts by telling readers to close the book. That's strange for a narrator. I'm inferring he is warning us because he has been hurt by this story, and that he is looking back on it, because he says what he wishes he'd done.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 2, at *envy* on p. 1: \"Percy says he *envies* readers who think this is fiction. I'll check the meaning in context: he says they can believe none of it happened. So envy must mean he wishes he could be like them. I'll confirm with the glossary: wishing you had what someone else has.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 3, at the school trouble (*expelled*, *probation*, *detention*, *threatened*): \"These words are all about getting in trouble. Context tells me *expelled* means kicked out of school, and the text says he has been kicked out of several. I'm predicting trouble follows him, and that it may not be his fault.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 4, at *dyslexia* and *immortal* (pp. 6–7): \"The text links *dyslexia* to Percy's struggle with reading, so I know it is a learning difference. And *immortal* ties back to our word parts: not dying. Gods in a school setting? That is where the modern myth begins.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words in the passage helped you figure out what *expelled* or *probation* means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text talks about Percy getting in trouble and leaving schools, so expelled must mean forced to leave. Probation sounds like a warning period where he must behave or something worse happens."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's first-person narration tell us about his past, and how can you tell?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It tells us he is looking back, because he says things like \"I didn't want to be a half-blood\" and warns readers. He already knows how the story turned out."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.6"],"stem":"What does the opening warning (\"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood...\") suggest about Percy as a narrator?","choices":[{"text":"He is telling the story after it happened and does not want readers to share his experience.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. His warning to close the book and his regret show he is narrating from the future with strong feelings about what happened."},{"text":"He is proud to be a half-blood and wants readers to join him.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses his message. He says being a half-blood is dangerous and tells readers to avoid it."},{"type":"x","text":"He has no feelings about the story and is only listing facts.","correct":false,"rationale":"His informal, sarcastic voice shows strong feelings, so this misreads his attitude."},{"text":"He is writing as a young child who does not know what will happen.","correct":false,"rationale":"He speaks from after the events, not as someone who doesn't yet know the outcome."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in following a first-person narrator and verifying new words in context during the read-aloud.","sayAsk":"Say: \"Percy is telling this story. He says *I*.\" Ask: \"Who is telling the story? How do you know?\" Frames: \"The narrator says ___, so I know ___.\" \"The word ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___.\" \"The text shows ___ when ___.\" Allow partners to retell Percy's warning in a home language first.","watchFor":"If students cannot follow the speaker, then point to the word *I* and have them find two more. If students give a meaning without evidence, then ask which words in the sentence helped. Success: students name a clue word and state a meaning in their own words."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: following Percy's narration and slang","tryThis":"Provide a short list of Percy's phrases with plain-language paraphrases to read before the read-aloud. Pause after each stop and have students restate in one sentence what Percy just said."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: narrator point of view","tryThis":"Ask students to explain what changes if the opening is rewritten in third person, and why Riordan chose first-person narration."}]}]},{"id":"lia-tone-word-choice","title":"Part B: How Percy's Word Choices Create Tone","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.6","L.6.4","L.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the first page or two of Chapter 1. Make a two-column chart. Column 1: a word or phrase that is informal or sarcastic. Column 2: what it shows about Percy's attitude and how it makes you feel about him. Find at least three."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Tone is the attitude a narrator shows. Informal words (like \"Look,\") sound like someone talking to you. Sarcasm says one thing and means another. Together they create a voice that feels honest, funny, and a little angry."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Model: \"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood.\" The word *Look* sounds like he is already annoyed and talking directly to me. It tells me he is blunt and doesn't want to be here, which makes me trust him and feel curious."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words or phrases make Percy's tone informal or sarcastic, and what attitude do they show?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When Percy says he *envies* readers who think this is fiction, it is sarcastic because he really means his life is hard. It shows he is bitter and wishes he were normal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is your first impression of Percy based on his tone?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My first impression is that he is honest, a little rebellious, and funny, but also scared. He says things plainly, like he doesn't care what adults think, but the warning shows he's worried."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy's choice of the word *normal* sound when he says it? What does that word connotation tell you about what he values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When he says normal, it sounds like something good and safe that he wishes he had. That tells me he values an ordinary, quiet life."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Add detail with adverbials. Revise one sentence from your chart to say **when**, **how**, or **why**. Example: \"Percy speaks bluntly at the start of the book because he wants to scare readers away.\""},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners evaluate language choices and add precise detail to sentences with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: \"Percy's words sound casual. We call this informal.\" Ask: \"Which word sounds like Percy is talking to you? How does it make you feel?\" Frames: \"Percy uses the word ___, which shows he feels ___.\" \"Percy speaks ___ (how) because ___ (why).\" \"At the beginning of the book, Percy ___ (when).\"","watchFor":"If students only say a word is \"funny,\" then ask what attitude lies behind the joke. If sentences stay bare, then prompt for how, when or why. Success: students link a specific word to an attitude and expand one sentence with an adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: identifying sarcasm and tone","tryThis":"Offer a tone-word bank (annoyed, honest, bitter, scared, funny) and have students pick one word per example, then say the evidence that supports it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: connotation","tryThis":"Ask students to compare *normal* and *ordinary* or *average*, and explain which word Percy might choose and why."}]}]},{"id":"lia-infer-predict-theme","title":"Part C: Hero or \"Problem\" Figure? Inferences, Predictions and an Emerging Theme","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","RL.6.5","L.6.6"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share and Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Think about what Percy says about \"normal\" kids and about himself. With a partner, fill in the chart: **Evidence from the text** | **What I infer about Percy's values or fears** | **Prediction: hero or \"problem\" figure?** Then write 3–4 sentences answering: How do Percy's comments show his values and fears about normal kids, and how might these pages be setting him up to become a hero or a problem figure in a modern myth?"},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"An inference is what you figure out by combining text evidence with what you already know. A theme is a big idea about life, not a plot summary. Today we are only noticing an *emerging* theme, one the book is starting to hint at."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy seem to value or fear when he talks about \"normal\" kids?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He seems to value being normal, because he says he envies people who think the story is fiction. He fears being different and being a half-blood, since he says it is dangerous and gets people killed."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why might a myth start with a hero who doesn't want to be one?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In myths, heroes often have to face things they didn't choose. Percy being reluctant and in trouble at school makes me think he'll be pushed into a big adventure, and people may see him as a problem before they see him as a hero."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What theme might be starting to emerge from these opening pages?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A possible theme is that being different can feel like a curse but may actually be a strength. Percy sees being different as a problem, but the story hints that his differences, like dyslexia and trouble in school, could matter."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Accept any theme grounded in evidence. Push students to separate summary (\"Percy gets in trouble\") from theme (\"being different can feel like a burden\"). Keep the theme tentative: it will be tested across the novel."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.2"],"stem":"Which statement best describes an emerging theme in the opening pages of Chapter 1?","choices":[{"text":"Being different can feel like a burden, even when it may hide something important.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. Percy wishes to be normal and describes his differences as dangerous, but the details hint that they may matter."},{"text":"Percy has been expelled from several schools.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a plot detail, not a theme. It supports a theme but does not state a big idea."},{"text":"Normal kids are always happier than kids with special abilities.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy envies normal kids, but the text does not claim they are always happier. This overstates his perspective."},{"text":"Schools are the best place for kids to learn about mythology.","correct":false,"rationale":"The text shows school mostly as a place of trouble for Percy and does not make this claim."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in making evidence-based inferences and predictions, and in distinguishing theme from summary.","sayAsk":"Say: \"We use the text plus our thinking to make an inference.\" Ask: \"What does the text say? What does it make you think?\" Frames: \"The text says ___, so I infer ___.\" \"Based on ___, I predict Percy will ___.\" \"A theme in these pages might be ___ because ___.\" Allow a home-language rehearsal before writing.","watchFor":"If students retell events, then ask: \"What bigger idea do these events show?\" If a prediction has no evidence, then ask which words in the text led to it. Success: students link a quoted detail to an inference and a prediction."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: moving from evidence to inference","tryThis":"Give the frame \"The text says ___. This makes me think ___ because ___.\" Have students say it to a partner before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: theme","tryThis":"Ask students to write two competing predictions (hero and problem figure), then decide which has stronger evidence and explain why."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students consolidate their first inference about Percy and connect today's work to the Performance Task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-exit-reflection","title":"Exit Reflection: First Impressions of Percy","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","L.6.4"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Connect to the Performance Task: \"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, you will explain a theme and support it with evidence. Today you started by noticing what Percy values and fears. That is where a theme begins.\""},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentences: \"Percy's tone in the opening is ___ because he uses the word or phrase ___. This shows he values ___ and fears ___. I predict he will become a ___ because ___.\" Then circle one vocabulary word you can now explain using word parts or context."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's tone in the opening is blunt and sarcastic because he uses the phrase \"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood.\" This shows he values being normal and fears being a half-blood. I predict he will become a reluctant hero because he doesn't choose this life but keeps getting pulled into it."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Students preview the next pages and a fable to prepare for explanatory writing and later comparison of stories that teach lessons.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-annotate","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Optional: (1) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1, pp. 9–15. Underline one detail that shows how Percy sees himself and star one example of his sarcastic or informal voice. (2) Read and annotate the excerpt from \"The Hare and the Lion.\" Note what each character does and what lesson the story might teach."}]}]}],"digest":null}}
